; Bank-0 sound-driver working state. Arrays are indexed by seven logical voices;
; slots 0..3 are music and 4..6 are effects. These are CPU RAM identities.
; 16-byte iNES header: mapper1, 128KiB PRG ROM, no CHR ROM or trainer. CHR graphics are transferred into cartridge CHR RAM; this header is not executable CPU storage.

; Thirty eight-byte instrument records. The voice setup consumers use the first six fields; the next rooted sequence independently bounds the array. The remaining repeated records have the same layout, although their natural selection is unproved.

; Voice sequence programs selected by four parallel directories. Commands are stop0, pattern1, repeat/jump2 and repeat setup3; operands and cursor advancement follow the sound interpreter. Roots and complete parsed successors bound this entire container.
; Thirty-one selected relative-offset arrays. A pattern ID indexes a little-endian displacement added to the selection's pattern base; these are not absolute CPU pointers.

; Pattern event streams: literal note/duration pairs, instrument changes and FF termination. Parsed note values are0..12 and instrument values0..26. All pointers and consumers require the sound bank0 view.
; Twenty-one FF bytes between the parsed final sound event and the sound entry. Repetition and neighboring boundaries support generic data; their original purpose is unknown.

; Consume the shifted sound request, then tick music voices 0..3 and effect voices 4..6. Zero means continue current streams; the high-bit request selects the effect group. Selection IDs and the exact request encoding remain uncertain.
; Reload music pattern bases/offset tables for the selected ID and initialize its four voices. Preserve effect-owned APU channels while changing music.
; Clear the previous effect channel claims, load the new effect tables and initialize three effect voices. The selected streams determine which hardware channels are claimed.
; A request is consumed once; ordinary later ticks retain the saved voice state.

; Four arrays of31 little-endian sequence pointers, followed by31 offset-array pointers and31 pattern bases. Trailing voice-table origins select each channel. The sound selector and pattern consumers establish the strides; directory entries do not prove every song was played.
; Tick active music slots in descending order. Unpack each saved cursor pair, process its duration/stream, and save the updated cursors.
; Apply the same stream interpreter to effect slots 6..4; their channel mask gives them priority over music writes.
; Initialize four music sequence pointers from the selection table, then retain their interpreter state.
; Initialize three effect sequence pointers; the shared initializer rebases their slot indices to 0..2.
; Persist sequence/pattern pointers and their independent byte cursors for voice X.
; Restore the working sequence/pattern pointers and cursors for voice X.
; Use twice the voice index plus the music selection as a pointer-table offset. This code assumes the corresponding bank-0 tables remain mapped.
; Rebase effect slot X by four, then use the effect selection to choose its sequence pointer.
; Read the selected sequence pointer, clear duration/hold/repeat state, mark the channel unassigned and activate the voice.

; Sequence byte 1 selects a pattern through a relative-offset table; byte 2 replaces the sequence cursor; byte 3 reads or decrements the repeat counter and restores the saved cursor until its final iteration. Other command values stop the voice. The bounded sequence/pattern graph is classified; natural selection of every root is unproved.
; Deactivate this voice and silence its hardware channel, subject to effect priority.
; The next sequence byte is an absolute byte offset within the same sequence, rather than a ROM pointer.
; Resolve a pattern index through the music/effect offset table and add that group's pattern base. Reset the pattern cursor and continue decoding events.

; Test the per-voice repeat count. Zero reads and saves a repeat offset/count; one decrements then skips the repeat operands. Larger counts decrement and restore the saved cursor before dispatching again.
; Restore this voice's saved sequence cursor and resume command dispatch.
; Save the repeat count from the stream, retaining the advanced cursor for sequence dispatch.
; Skip the three repeat operands and resume the sequence after the completed repetition.
; A negative pattern byte selects an eight-byte instrument record at CPU $8000. Its first fields supply pitch bias and hardware channel; later output paths consume control/timer flags.
; While a duration remains, only handle note release and decrement it. Otherwise decode the next pattern event; $FF returns to the outer sequence interpreter.

; Nonnegative events pack note index in the low nibble and pitch shift in the high nibble. The following byte indexes a duration table and carries hold bit $40. Negative events change instrument; $FF returns to sequence commands.
; Look up a 16-bit note timer, right-shift by the adjusted pitch field when positive, then send it to the selected APU channel. Zero/negative shifts leave the table value intact.
; The duration byte also supplies a hold flag; retain it so the next tick decides whether to release the note.
; On the final tick, release unless the hold flag is set; then decrement the remaining duration.
; Skip unassigned channels. Music may not silence a channel claimed by an effect; effects update their claim mask before clearing the APU enable bit.
; Effects claim their hardware channel; music writes are suppressed while an effect owns it. Enable the channel, then dispatch channel IDs 0/1/2/other to pulse1/pulse2/triangle/noise registers.
; Merge adjusted volume with instrument control, write sweep, and combine the computed timer with instrument length flags.
; Write the second pulse channel using the same instrument/timer layout as pulse1.
; Adjust the triangle control byte, then write the timer and instrument length flags.
; Use the timer low nibble as the noise period, combined with instrument mode flags. No tonal high-timer write is needed.
; Add the signed global volume adjustment to the low control nibble and clamp to 0..15. Preserve the original upper control bits.

; Adjust the triangle control byte by pairs of volume steps: positive adjustment rotates in set bits; negative adjustment shifts right. Preserve the caller's voice index X. Exact loudness correspondence is uncertain.

; Per-object palette color triples consumed through the object palette selector. Four-byte RAM slots retain a separate shared/background cell; these ROM records supply the other colors.
; Copy $84 bytes from the bank-local template to RAM ScoreRecordBuffer..$0483. Later code treats these as ten twelve-byte score/name records.
; Busy-wait on PPUSTATUS bit 7, then read it again to clear the latch. This polls the PPU rather than the frame interrupt flag.
; Wait for vblank, clear scroll and PPUCTRL, then enable background/sprite rendering with PPUMASK $1E. Keep software register shadows synchronized.
; Clear PPU control/mask at vblank, then fill and DMA the sprite page. This prepares a screen change without visible sprite remnants.

; Preserve the six-byte current score on the stack, change the screen resources, draw ten score/name records and insert the current score. The classified path later waits for input or timeout; name-entry paths have gaps.
; Copy 32 palette bytes to PPU $3F00 before drawing the score table.
; Populate the score screen attribute cells with $55/$AA patterns. PPUDATA reads deliberately advance the VRAM address between the selected cells.
; Each twelve-byte RAM record has six glyph bytes and six decimal digits. Render a row, advance the PPU destination by 32 tiles, and stop after ten records.
; Track whether any prior digit was nonzero; replace leading zeroes with tile $1E, while always drawing the final digit. Digit tiles begin at $1F.
; Y=$78 denotes no insertion. That path enables the score display and skips keyboard name entry.

; Build a sprite keyboard cursor and six character slots. A selects the highlighted glyph, the delete glyph backs up one position, and the finish glyph exits. Direction lookup deltas move the cursor only inside the keyboard bounds; direct OAM DMA animates each step while waiting for controller release. The accepted characters are also written to the score-name buffer.
; Poll input for up to 100 vblanks, exiting early on either mask-$30 button. Restore the saved score and finish clearing the record state before returning.
; Finish clearing the record slots and clear the score-screen state before returning.
; Three sixteen-cell delta arrays for keyboard X, Y and glyph selection. Direction bits index the arrays; the name-entry routine bounds the resulting cursor before changing its sprite position.
; Fill thirty rows of 32 tiles with blank tile $1E, then clear 64 attribute bytes. Leaves the PPU write address immediately after this nametable.

; Score/name display records, palette values and encoded text. Nearby score drawing and keyboard glyph consumers establish their data roles. Individual decorative cells remain unnamed where the exact original display grouping is unresolved.

; Use RAM $54/$55 as the string pointer and $56/$57 as the PPU destination. Nonnegative bytes pass through the glyph mapper. $FF ends; other negative bytes advance the destination by their low seven bits. Strings therefore encode both text and skips.
; Stop at $FF; otherwise update the saved 16-bit destination, rewrite PPUADDR and resume at the next encoded byte. The arithmetic preserves the carry convention from the terminator comparison.
; Fill CPU page $03 with $FF and transfer it to OAM using OAMDMA page 3. The same RAM page is the software sprite buffer.

; Compare the six score bytes lexicographically with existing records, searching from the final record. Equal bytes continue the comparison; insertion shifts lower records and stores the current score. Name entry is handled separately.
; Compare record score bytes at $03FA+Y with current score $1B+X from most significant to least significant. Equality continues through all six bytes.
; Fill the remaining score-row sprite tiles, move backward by the row stride, and continue until every row is prepared.
; Copy the current six-byte score to the selected record and return the insertion offset in Y.
